title: LLM Multi-Agent Systems Are Vulnerable to Herding and Runaway Cascades
content:
Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence
  [Submitted on 22 Oct 2026]
Title:LLM Multi-Agent Systems Are Vulnerable to Herding and Runaway Cascades
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:Large language models (LLMs) increasingly operate in multi-agent systems where they collaborate by responding to others' choices, creating endogenous feedback loops with vulnerability to social influence, herding behavior and runaway cascades. Following the design of the classic Music Lab experiment, we tested this vulnerability in large populations of LLM agents that recommended unfamiliar songs, with or without exposure to cumulative recommendation counts. Exposure led to runaway cascades that generated extreme and unpredictable collective recommendations increasingly divergent from a song's intrinsic appeal. Compared to humans, LLM populations were generally far more susceptible to herding behavior, and unlike humans, LLM cascades were less able to self-correct. This vulnerability has implications for multi-agent collaboration in recommender systems, automated evaluation, complex problem-solving, and unauthorized conspiracies.

report.summary: A Music Lab-style study finds LLM agent populations herd far more than humans when shown cumulative choices, producing runaway, unpredictable recommendation cascades that rarely self-correct.
report.background: LLM multi-agent systems increasingly let models collaborate by observing and responding to one another's outputs. That design creates endogenous feedback loops: early choices become signals that shape later choices, much like social influence in cultural markets. The classic Music Lab experiment showed that exposing people to cumulative popularity counts can amplify inequality and unpredictability in song rankings. This paper adapts that design to large populations of LLM agents recommending unfamiliar songs. The result matters because agent frameworks are moving into recommender systems, automated evaluation, complex problem-solving, and other settings where collective LLM behavior can compound errors rather than average them out.
key_points: The study adapts the classic Music Lab design: large populations of LLM agents recommend unfamiliar songs, either independently or with exposure to cumulative recommendation counts. Exposure is the trigger. Without social information, collective recommendations track intrinsic appeal more closely; with it, early choices become self-reinforcing signals.

LLM populations are generally far more susceptible to herding than human participants. Small initial advantages can snowball into extreme and unpredictable collective rankings, increasingly divergent from a song's intrinsic appeal. The cascade is not just noise; it reflects social feedback dominating independent judgment.

Unlike human crowds in the original experiment, LLM cascades are less able to self-correct. Once a runaway trajectory forms, agents tend to reinforce it rather than recover. That makes errors persistent and potentially harder to detect in deployed multi-agent workflows.

The authors flag implications for recommender systems, automated evaluation, complex problem-solving, and unauthorized conspiracies. In each case, agents responding to other agents can amplify bias, manipulate rankings, or coordinate on poor answers without any single model being explicitly instructed to do so.
report.impact: For the AI industry, the finding challenges the assumption that multi-agent collaboration reliably improves quality through debate or consensus. Systems that expose agents to popularity, confidence, or prior outputs need diversity-preserving designs, independent sampling, randomization, circuit breakers, and audit trails. Developers should test agents under social-information conditions, not just isolated benchmarks, because evaluation scores may be contaminated by herding. Recommender systems and marketplaces face distorted rankings and manipulation risk; automated evaluators may converge on flawed judgments. For regular users, the risk is echo chambers, unstable recommendations, and false consensus presented as collective intelligence. The paper does not show every multi-agent system fails, but it makes cascade risk a first-class design and safety concern.
report.tools: To follow up, watch agent-simulation and orchestration frameworks such as Microsoft AutoGen, LangGraph, CrewAI, and DeepMind Concordia; Mesa for agent-based modeling; AgentVerse; and reproducible Music Lab-style test harnesses. Use them to compare independent versus social-information conditions, add cascade breakers and audit logs, and stress-test collective LLM behavior before deployment.
